Here's a five-night plan for two, no pork, everything 30 minutes or under. I've made a few assumptions — no other dietary limits, ordinary grocery-store ingredients, and a willingness to cook fresh most nights — so say the word if any of those are off and I'll swap dishes.

Two things are deliberately engineered in: Tuesday's rice becomes Friday's fried rice, and Wednesday and Friday share the same aromatics, so you're not buying ginger twice.

## The week

**Monday — Sheet-pan gnocchi with chicken sausage and peppers** (25 min, one pan)
Toss a package of shelf-stable gnocchi (no boiling) with sliced chicken or turkey sausage, a bell pepper, a pint of cherry tomatoes, olive oil, salt. 425°F, 20–22 min, stir once. Basil or parmesan at the end. The gnocchi crisps on the outside and goes pillowy inside.

**Tuesday — Miso-butter salmon, rice, smashed cucumbers** (20 min)
Rice on first (make a double batch — this is Friday's dinner). Mash 1 tbsp white miso into 2 tbsp soft butter, smear on two salmon fillets, roast 400°F for 12 min. Meanwhile smash a cucumber, toss with rice vinegar, a little sesame oil, salt, and flaky chile if you like heat.

**Wednesday — Seared chicken thighs with lemony white beans and spinach** (25 min)
Salt boneless thighs, sear skin-side down 7–8 min undisturbed, flip 4 min, rest. In the same pan: garlic, a rinsed can of cannellini, a splash of chicken stock, big handful of spinach, lemon juice off the heat. Slice the chicken over the beans.

**Thursday — Ground beef tacos with quick cabbage slaw** (20 min)
Brown a pound of beef with cumin, chili powder, oregano, a spoon of tomato paste. Slaw: shredded cabbage, lime, salt, a little mayo or sour cream. Warm corn tortillas directly over a burner if you have gas.

**Friday — Egg fried rice with whatever's left** (15 min)
Cold Tuesday rice is the whole trick — fresh rice steams instead of frying. Hot oil, scramble two eggs and set aside, then ginger and scallion, frozen peas and carrots, the rice pressed flat for a minute to crisp, eggs back in, soy sauce and a few drops of sesame oil.

## Pork to watch for

The obvious swaps are easy, but three things hide it:

- **Sausage** — most Italian and breakfast sausage is pork. Buy one labeled chicken or turkey.
- **Refried beans and some tortillas** — often made with lard (*manteca*). Check the label, or just use whole black beans.
- **Anything calling for bacon or pancetta** as a base — smoked turkey or a spoon of smoked paprika gets you most of the way there.

If the no-pork rule is religious rather than a preference, there may be more to it — halal or kosher sourcing for the beef and chicken, or avoiding wine and mirin in cooking. Worth asking your partner; it'd change the beef and the fried rice seasoning, not the overall plan.

## Shopping list

**Proteins** — 2 salmon fillets, 4 boneless chicken thighs, 1 lb ground beef, 1 package chicken/turkey sausage

**Produce** — 2 bell peppers, 1 pint cherry tomatoes, 2 cucumbers, 1 bag spinach, 1 small green cabbage, 1 bunch scallions, ginger, garlic, 2 lemons, 2 limes, basil

**Pantry/refrigerated** — shelf-stable gnocchi, white miso, butter, 1 can cannellini beans, rice, rice vinegar, sesame oil, soy sauce, corn tortillas, tomato paste, chicken stock, frozen peas and carrots, eggs, cumin, chili powder, oregano

Want me to shift any night vegetarian, or rebalance if you'd rather cook three times and eat leftovers the other two?

Here's the sheet-pan gnocchi — it's a Food Network Kitchen recipe (widely credited to Ali Slagle). Food Network blocks automated fetching, so I pulled the ingredient list from a mirror and the directions from the indexed recipe text; the link is below if you want to confirm against the original.

## Crispy Sheet-Pan Gnocchi with Sausage and Peppers
*Food Network Kitchen — serves 4*

**Ingredients**
- 1 lb sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, crumbled
- 1 tsp dried oregano
- ¼ tsp crushed red pepper flakes
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 small green bell pepper, thinly sliced
- 1 small red bell pepper, thinly sliced
- 1 small yellow bell pepper, thinly sliced
- 1 small red onion, thinly sliced
- 2 tbsp olive oil, divided
- Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
- Two 14-oz cans cherry tomatoes
- One 17.5-oz package potato gnocchi
- ¼ cup grated Parmesan, plus more for serving
- ¼ cup fresh parsley leaves, chopped

**Directions**
1. Preheat the oven to 425°F.
2. Toss the sausage, oregano, red pepper flakes, garlic, bell peppers, onion, 1 tbsp of the olive oil, 1 tsp salt, and a few grinds of black pepper on a sheet pan. Pour the cherry tomatoes over top and gently shake the pan a few times to distribute evenly.
3. Bake until the sausage is cooked through and the vegetables are soft, 18 to 20 minutes.
4. Meanwhile, toss the gnocchi with the Parmesan, the remaining 1 tbsp olive oil, and ½ tsp salt.
5. Turn the oven to broil. Sprinkle the gnocchi over the sausage and vegetables and broil until dark golden brown, 3 to 5 minutes.
6. Divide among 4 plates and sprinkle with parsley and more Parmesan.

## Changes for your week

**The sausage.** Sweet Italian sausage is pork. Swap in 1 lb of chicken or turkey Italian sausage — if it's in links, slice it into coins rather than crumbling it, since poultry sausage doesn't hold together as well loose. The oregano and red pepper flakes in the recipe are doing the work that pork fat normally would, so keep both.

**Halving it.** Use ½ lb sausage, one bell pepper instead of three, half the onion, one 14-oz can of tomatoes, and a 12-oz package of gnocchi (the common size). Keep the full 2 tbsp of oil and ¼ cup Parmesan — the gnocchi needs the fat to crisp. Use a smaller pan or push everything to one half of a full sheet; crowding is what makes gnocchi steam instead of brown.

**Two honest notes.** This uses *canned* cherry tomatoes, not the fresh pint I listed in the shopping plan — canned gives you a saucier result. Either works; fresh will be drier and more roasted. And the real time is closer to 35 minutes with prep, not 25. If you want it under 30, slice the peppers and onion the night before, or buy pre-sliced.
